p.src: The tale tells how Tripitaka of the Tang, steadfast in his devotion—not to mention the protection of the heavenly gods—was guided onward even by the spirits of plants and trees. After a refined gathering that lasted the night, he escaped the thorny brambles, with no more vines or gourds to entangle him. The four travelers continued westward for a long while. Winter was ending, and the season of spring had arrived:

p.src: Master and disciples, too, sought fragrant blossoms and trod the green, proceeding leisurely at the horse's pace. As they traveled, they suddenly saw a lofty mountain which, viewed from afar, seemed to meet the sky. Tripitaka raised his whip and pointed. “Wukong, who knows how high that mountain may be? It seems to touch the blue heavens and thrust into the azure firmament.” Pilgrim replied, “Does not an ancient poem say, ‘Above it there is only heaven; no other mountain stands its equal’? That merely means the mountain is exceedingly high and none can compare with it. How could it truly touch heaven?” Bajie said, “If it does not touch heaven, why is Mount Kunlun called the Pillar of Heaven?” Pilgrim said, “You do not understand. Since ancient times it has been said that ‘heaven is incomplete in the northwest.’ Mount Kunlun lies in the northwest, the position of Qian. Thus it conveys the idea of propping up heaven and filling the empty sky, and so was named the Pillar of Heaven.” Friar Sand laughed. “Elder Brother, do not tell him such fine things. He will learn them and use them to confound other people. Let us keep going. Once we have climbed that mountain, we shall know how high it is.”

p.src: At the sight of it, Tripitaka of the Tang was alarmed. But Sun the Pilgrim possessed immense magic powers. With his single gold-banded cudgel and one thunderous roar, he frightened away wolves, tigers, leopards, and other beasts, opened a path, and led his master straight up the high mountain. After crossing the ridge and descending to level ground on its western side, they suddenly saw auspicious light glowing and colored mists swirling. Amid them stood towers, terraces, halls, and pavilions, while the faint, melodious sounds of bells and chimes floated through the air. Tripitaka said, “Disciples, look and see what sort of place that is.” Pilgrim raised his head, shaded his eyes with one hand, and looked carefully. What a splendid place it was! Indeed:

p.src: When Pilgrim had finished looking, he reported, “Master, that place is a monastery. Yet I cannot understand why, amid its holy light and auspicious haze, there is also an air of menace. Judging by this scene, it resembles Thunderclap Monastery, but the road is wrong. When we reach it, we must not enter rashly, lest we fall victim to some murderous scheme.” The Tang Monk said, “Since it bears the signs of Thunderclap, could it not be Vulture Peak itself? Do not thwart my sincere devotion and delay the purpose for which I came.” Pilgrim said, “No, no. I have traveled the road to Vulture Peak several times. How could this be that road?” Bajie said, “Even if it is not, some worthy person must surely live there.” Friar Sand said, “There is no need for so much suspicion. This road must pass before its gate; once we see it, we shall know whether it is genuine or not.” Pilgrim said, “Wujing speaks wisely.”

p.src: The elder urged his horse forward until he reached the monastery gate. Seeing the three large characters “Thunderclap Monastery,” he tumbled from his horse in panic, fell to the ground, and cursed, “You wretched macaque! You have nearly been the death of me! Here stands Thunderclap Monastery before our very eyes, yet you still tried to deceive me.” Pilgrim smiled placatingly. “Do not be angry, Master. Look again. There are four characters over the gate. Why have you read only three and then blamed me?” Trembling, the elder climbed to his feet and looked again. There were indeed four characters: “Lesser Thunderclap Monastery.” Tripitaka said, “Even if it is the Lesser Thunderclap Monastery, there must surely be a Buddha within. The sutras speak of three thousand Buddhas, and I imagine they do not all dwell in one place: Guanyin is in the Southern Sea, Samantabhadra on Mount Emei, and Manjusri on Mount Wutai. I wonder which Buddha’s sacred precinct this may be. The ancients said, ‘Where there is a Buddha, there is scripture; no region is without its treasure.’ We should go inside.” Pilgrim said, “We must not enter. This place promises little good and much evil. If disaster strikes, do not blame me.” Tripitaka said, “Even if there is no Buddha, there must at least be an image of one. My heart’s vow as a disciple is to worship every Buddha I encounter. How could I blame you?”

p.src: He immediately ordered Bajie to fetch his cassock and changed into his monk’s cap. Having put his robes and headgear in order, he stepped forward. A voice called from inside the monastery gate: “Tang Monk, you have come from the Eastern Land to pay homage to our Buddha. Why are you still so remiss?” On hearing this, Tripitaka immediately bowed down; Bajie kowtowed as well, and Friar Sand also sank to his knees. Only the Great Sage remained behind, leading the horse and attending to the luggage. As soon as they passed through the second gate, they saw the Great Hall of the Tathagata. Outside the hall, beneath the jeweled terrace, were arrayed five hundred arhats, three thousand guardians of the faith, four vajra warriors, eight bodhisattvas, nuns, lay devotees, and countless holy monks and Daoist adepts. Fragrant flowers truly bloomed in splendor, while auspicious vapors shimmered in a profusion of colors. So overawed were the elder, Bajie, and Friar Sand that they advanced to the sacred terrace, bowing at every step. Pilgrim, however, openly refused to bow. Then a stern voice cried from the lotus throne, “Sun Wukong! Why do you not bow before the Tathagata?” Pilgrim had been examining everything closely and now saw that it was false. He dropped the horse’s reins and the luggage, drew his cudgel, and shouted, “You vile beasts are exceedingly bold! How dare you falsely shelter behind the Buddha’s name and sully the Tathagata’s pure virtue? Do not try to flee!” Gripping the cudgel in both hands, he swung it and charged forward to strike. Just then there came a clang from midair, and a pair of golden cymbals dropped down, closing around Pilgrim from head to foot and trapping him inside. Zhu Bajie and Friar Sand hurriedly raised rake and staff, but the arhats, guardians, holy monks, and Daoist adepts swarmed forward and surrounded them. Taken unawares, both were captured. They seized Tripitaka as well. All three were wound about with ropes, bound tightly, and securely fastened.

p.src: It turned out that the figure posing as the Buddha on the lotus throne was a demon king, while all the arhats and others were lesser fiends. He put away the semblance of the Buddha and revealed his demonic form once more. He had the other three carried into the rear and locked away. As for Pilgrim, he left him sealed within the golden cymbals, never to be released, and set them upon the jeweled terrace, decreeing that within three days and nights he would dissolve into blood and pus. Once he had dissolved, they would steam the other three in an iron cage and feast upon them. This was truly a case of:

There they kept everything under the strictest guard, of which we shall speak no further for now.

p.src: Now the Pilgrim was shut inside the golden cymbals. It was pitch-dark, and the stifling heat made sweat pour from his whole body. He shoved left and rammed right, but could not get out. In desperation he struck wildly with his iron staff, but could not budge them in the least. At his wits' end, he strained outward with all his body, intending to burst the golden cymbals apart. He made a magic sign and grew hundreds of fathoms tall; but the golden cymbals grew with him, leaving not the smallest crack or glimmer of light. Then he made another sign and shrank himself until he was as tiny as a mustard seed; but the cymbals shrank with him, without so much as a pinhole anywhere. He breathed an immortal breath upon his iron staff and cried, “Change!” It at once became like a banner pole and braced the golden cymbals apart. Then he selected two long hairs from the back of his head, plucked them out, and cried, “Change!” They instantly became five-fluted, plum-blossom-headed drills. Placing them beneath the staff, he bored a thousand times, but produced only a ringing clang and failed to pierce even the slightest bit. Growing desperate, the Pilgrim made a magic sign and recited the spell, “Om, purity throughout the Dharma realm; Qian, origin, prosperity, benefit, constancy.” He thereby summoned the Guardians of the Five Quarters, the Six Dings and Six Jias, and the eighteen monastery guardians. From outside the golden cymbals they said, “Great Sage, we are all protecting your master so that the demons cannot harm him. Why have you summoned us?” The Pilgrim said, “My master refused to heed my warning, so even if they kill him, he will have only himself to blame. Just use your powers at once to prise open these cymbals and let me out; then we can decide what to do. No light enters here, and my whole body is feverishly hot. Will this place not smother me to death?” The gods truly tried to lift the cymbals, but they seemed grown together and could not be moved a fraction. The Golden-Headed Guardian said, “Great Sage, we do not know what kind of treasure these cymbals may be. Their upper and lower halves have fused into one piece. This humble god's strength is too slight to lift them.” The Pilgrim said, “Inside here I have used every power I know, yet I too could not move them.”

p.src: On hearing this, the Guardian ordered the Six Ding gods to protect Tang Sanzang, the Six Jia gods to watch over the golden cymbals, and the monastery guardians to keep guard before and behind. He himself mounted an auspicious beam of light and, in an instant, rushed through the Southern Gate of Heaven. Without waiting to be summoned, he went straight beneath the Hall of Miraculous Mist, prostrated himself before the Jade Emperor, and reported, “My lord, your servant is an emissary of the Guardians of the Five Quarters. The Great Sage Equal to Heaven is now escorting Tang Sanzang to fetch the scriptures, and on the road they came upon a mountain bearing a place called the Little Thunderclap Monastery. Tang Sanzang mistook it for Vulture Peak and entered to worship, but it was a counterfeit set up by a demon. The creature trapped master and disciples and shut the Great Sage inside a pair of golden cymbals, leaving him no way forward or back. He is on the verge of death, so I have come especially to report this.” The Jade Emperor immediately issued a decree: “Dispatch the constellations of the Twenty-eight Lunar Mansions. Have them hurry to end this calamity and subdue the demon.”

p.src: The stars dared not delay. Accompanying the Guardian, they left the Gate of Heaven and arrived within the monastery gates at about the second watch of the night. The demons, great and small, had been rewarded by their old king for capturing Tang Sanzang and had all gone to sleep. Without raising any alarm, the stars gathered outside the cymbals and announced, “Great Sage, we are the Twenty-eight Lunar Mansions sent by the Jade Emperor, and we have come to rescue you.” The Pilgrim was delighted to hear this and told them, “Strike it apart with your weapons, and Old Monkey will come straight out.” The stars replied, “We dare not strike it. This object is a treasure of solid gold. A blow is sure to make it ring, and the sound would rouse the demons, making your rescue all the harder. Let us use our weapons to prise it open. The moment you see the least glimmer of light in there, make your escape.” The Pilgrim said, “Just so.” Then behold them: those with spears used spears, those with swords used swords, those with sabres used sabres, and those with axes used axes; some shouldered, some lifted, some heaved, and some prised. They worked until the third watch, yet it remained utterly unmoved, as though cast whole in a single piece. Inside, the Pilgrim peered east and west, crawling this way and rolling that, but could not see the faintest glimmer of light.

p.src: The Horned Wood Dragon said, “Great Sage, do not be impatient. Judging by this treasure, it must be a wish-responsive object and is surely able to transform. From inside, feel with your hands along the seam where the halves meet. I shall force the tip of my horn through it. Then you can transform yourself and slip out wherever it loosens.” The Pilgrim followed his advice and began feeling all around inside. The star spirit made his body small, until the tip of his horn was as fine as a needle, and pushed it into the seam between the cymbals. Pitifully, only after exerting a thousand catties of strength did he manage to pierce through to the inside. Then he worked magic upon his own body and horn, crying, “Grow! Grow! Grow!” The horn grew until it was as thick as a bowl. Yet the mouths of the cymbals behaved not like cast metal but like living flesh: they closed tightly around the Horned Wood Dragon's horn, leaving not the finest crack on any side. The Pilgrim felt the horn and cried, “This will not do. There is not a hair's breadth of looseness above or below. There is no other way. Endure a little pain and carry me out with you.” What a Great Sage! He at once changed the gold-banded staff into a steel drill, bored a hole in the tip of the horn, shrank himself to the size of a mustard seed, wriggled into the hole and crouched there, crying, “Pull your horn out! Pull your horn out!” The star spirit expended untold strength before he finally pulled it free. His strength exhausted and sinews limp, he collapsed to the ground.

p.src: The Pilgrim crawled out of the hole in the tip of his horn, resumed his true form, drew his iron staff, and brought it down upon the cymbals with a clang like a bronze mountain collapsing and a golden mine bursting open. Alas, that Buddhist vessel was smashed into hundreds upon hundreds of fragments of gold. The Twenty-eight Lunar Mansions were startled into confusion, the hair of the Guardians of the Five Quarters stood on end, and every demon, great and small, awoke from its dreams. The old demon king woke in alarm, sprang up, threw on his clothes, beat the drum, mustered his demons, and had each take up a weapon. By then dawn was about to break. They surged beneath the jeweled platform and saw Sun the Pilgrim and the assembled stars standing around the shattered golden cymbals. The demon king turned pale with shock. He immediately commanded, “Underlings! Shut the front gate tight! Let no one escape!”

p.src: Hearing this, the Pilgrim gathered the host of stars, mounted the clouds, and leapt into the highest heavens. The demon king gathered up the fragments of gold, arrayed his demon troops, and drew them up outside the mountain gate. The demon king was filled with hatred. Having no other recourse, he donned his armour, took up a short, flexible wolf-tooth club, came out of his camp, and shouted, “Sun the Pilgrim! A true man does not flee far away. Come down at once and exchange three bouts with me!” Unable to contain himself, the Pilgrim led the stars down from the clouds to see what manner of creature the demon was. This is what he saw:

Unable to contain himself, the Pilgrim led the stars down from the clouds to see what manner of creature the demon was.
This is what he saw:

p.src: The Pilgrim raised his iron staff and shouted, “What manner of monster are you, that you dare impersonate the Buddha, seize this mountain, and set up a sham Little Thunderclap Monastery?” The demon king replied, “This monkey does not even know my name, yet he has come here to trespass upon my immortal mountain. This place is called the Little Western Heaven. Through cultivation I attained the true fruit, and Heaven bestowed these precious halls and jeweled towers upon me. My name is the Old Buddha Yellow Brows. The people here do not know that; they call me only Great King Yellow Brows or Grandfather Yellow Brows. I have long known that you were journeying westward and possessed some skill, so I displayed these images and powers to lure your master inside, intending to wager a contest with you. If you can defeat me, I shall spare master and disciples and let you attain the true fruit; but if you cannot, I shall beat you all to death, then go myself to see the Tathagata, fetch the scriptures, and bring their true fruit to China.” The Pilgrim laughed. “Fiend, spare me your boasting. If you want a wager, come quickly and taste my staff!” Delighted, the demon king met him with his spiked club. A fine battle it was:

p.src: The two fought for fifty rounds without either gaining the victory. At the mountain gate gongs sounded and drums thundered, while the demons shouted and waved their banners. On the other side, the celestial troops of the Twenty-Eight Lunar Mansions and the holy Guardians of the Five Regions shouldered their weapons and charged with a shout, surrounding the demon chief. The demons outside the gate were so terrified that they could no longer beat the drums, and their trembling, weakened hands could not strike the gongs. The old demon remained utterly unafraid, wielding his spiked club in one hand to hold off the celestial host; with the other he untied an old white cloth bag from his waist and tossed it upward. With a sharp whoosh, he swept Great Sage Sun, the Twenty-Eight Mansions, and the Guardians of the Five Regions into the bag together. Slipping it over his shoulder, he turned and strode away. All the lesser demons returned jubilantly in triumph. The old demon ordered his minions to fetch thirty or fifty hempen ropes, opened the bag, and had each captive taken out and bound in turn. Every one of them had limp bones and numb sinews, and their skin was shriveled and wrinkled. Once bound, they were carried to the rear and, without distinction, all flung to the ground. The demon king then ordered a banquet and drank heartily from dawn until dusk, when the feast finally ended and all retired to their quarters. We shall say no more of them.

p.src: Hearing this, the Pilgrim felt secret pity and thought, “Though Master refused to heed my words and has now met with this calamity, even amid his suffering he still remembers old Sun. While the night is still and the demons sleep, with no one keeping watch, I had better free everyone so that we may escape with our lives.”

p.src: What a Great Sage! Employing the art of escaping the body, he shrank himself, slipped free of the ropes, went to the Tang Monk’s side, and whispered, “Master.” Recognizing his voice, the elder cried, “How did you come here?” In a whisper, the Pilgrim recounted everything that had happened. The elder was overjoyed. “Disciple, quickly save me! From now on, I shall leave all matters to you and never insist upon my own way again.” The Pilgrim set to work, first freeing his master, and then Bajie and Sha Monk. He then released every one of the Twenty-Eight Mansions and the Guardians of the Five Regions. He brought over the horse as well and told them to hurry out first. They had just gone through the gate when he realized that he did not know where the luggage was, so he went back to search for it. The Horned Wood Dragon said, “You value possessions and slight people! Having saved your master, you have done enough. Why search for the luggage as well?” The Pilgrim replied, “People are important, certainly, but the robe and alms bowl are more important still. The bundle contains our travel rescript, the brocade cassock, and the purple-gold alms bowl, all supreme treasures of the Buddhist faith. How could we abandon them?” Bajie said, “Brother, you go and search for it. We shall wait for you on the road ahead.” See how the assembled stars clustered around the Tang Monk and, using arts of transport and their divine powers together, raised a gust of wind that swept them beyond the walls. They hastened to the main road, descended the mountainside, and encamped on level ground to wait.

p.src: At about the third watch, Great Sage Sun stole softly inside, only to find that every successive doorway was tightly secured. He climbed to the top of a tall tower and found that all its windows were closed. He wanted to descend inside, but fearing the window lattice would make a sound, dared not push it open. Forming a spell with his fingers, he shook himself and changed into an immortal rat, commonly called a bat. And what did he look like?

And what did he look like?

p.src: He squeezed in beneath the rafters through an unsealed gap under the tiles, passed through door after door, and reached the inner chambers. There, beneath a window on the third level, he saw a shimmering ray of fine light. It was neither lamplight nor candlelight, neither the glow of a firefly, nor the gleam of sunset clouds or a flash of lightning. Half flying and half hopping, he approached the window and saw that the radiance came from the bundle. The demon had stripped the Tang Monk of his cassock and, without even folding it, had stuffed it untidily into the bundle. That cassock was a Buddhist treasure, adorned with wish-fulfilling pearls, mani jewels, red agate, purple coral, relics, and night-shining pearls; hence its radiance shone through. Delighted to find the robe and bowl, he resumed his true form, seized the bundle, and, without troubling whether the carrying ropes lay straight, hoisted it onto his shoulder and started downstairs. Unexpectedly, one end slipped free and fell with a thud upon the floorboards, making a tremendous crash. Alas! What a mischance! As ill luck would have it, the old demon was sleeping downstairs. The noise woke him, and he sprang up shouting wildly, “Someone is here! Someone is here!” All the demons, great and small, arose, lit lamps and torches, and went shouting to search front and rear. One came to report, “The Tang Monk has escaped!” Another reported, “The Pilgrim and all the others have escaped too!” The old demon urgently issued an order: “Guard every gate closely!” Hearing this, the Pilgrim feared being caught in the demon’s snare again. Unable to carry the bundle properly, he turned a somersault, leaped out through the tower window, and fled.

p.src: The demon searched everywhere but could not find the Tang Monk and his companions. Seeing that dawn was near, he took up his club and led his horde in pursuit. There below the mountainside he saw the Twenty-Eight Mansions, the Guardians of the Five Regions, and the other gods encamped amid billowing clouds and mist. The demon king roared, “Where do you think you are going? Here I come!” The Horned Wood Flood Dragon hurriedly called, “Brothers, the monster is coming!” The Necked Gold Dragon, Rooted Earth Bat, Chambered Sun Hare, Heart Moon Fox, Tail Fire Tiger, Winnowing Water Leopard, Dipper Wood Xiezhi, Ox Gold Ox, Girl Earth Raccoon Dog, Emptiness Sun Rat, Rooftop Moon Swallow, Encampment Fire Pig, Wall Water Beast, Straddling Wood Wolf, Bond Gold Dog, Stomach Earth Boar, Hairy Head Sun Rooster, Net Moon Crow, Turtle Beak Fire Monkey, Three Stars Water Ape, Well Wood Wild Dog, Ghost Gold Ram, Willow Earth Roebuck, Star Sun Horse, Extended Net Moon Deer, Wings Fire Snake, and Chariot Water Worm led the Gold-Headed and Silver-Headed Guardians, the gods of the Six Jia and Six Ding, and the monastery guardians. Together with Bajie and Sha Monk—without Tang Sanzang, and having left the White Dragon Horse behind—they all brandished their weapons and surged forward as one. Seeing them, the demon king gave a cold chuckle and sounded a whistle. Four or five thousand demons, great and small, each fierce and powerful, appeared and joined in a chaotic battle on the western slope. A fine battle it was:

p.src: The demon fought with redoubled ferocity and led his horde forward in a sweeping assault.

p.src: Just as the battle hung undecided, they suddenly heard Pilgrim cry out, “Old Monkey is here!” Bajie went to meet him and asked, “What of the luggage?” Pilgrim replied, “Old Monkey barely escaped with his life—how can you still ask about the luggage?” Wujing, gripping his precious staff, said, “No time for talk. Quickly, let us fight the fiend!” The stellar gods, the Guardians of the Faith, the gods of the cyclical signs, and the rest were surrounded by the horde of fiends and fighting desperately at the heart of the encirclement, while the old demon came swinging his cudgel at the three disciples. Pilgrim, Bajie, and Wujing set to with staff, rake, and wand, brandishing their weapons to hold him off. They truly fought until earth was dark and heaven dim, yet still could gain no victory. They fought until the sun sank behind the western mountains and the moon rose above the eastern sea. Seeing that night had fallen, the demon gave a whistle and ordered all his fiends to stay alert; then he took out his treasure. Sun Wukong saw it clearly: the monster untied the cloth bag from his waist and held it in his hand. Pilgrim cried, “This is bad! Run!” With no time to look after Bajie, Wujing, or the assembled gods, he turned a somersault and leapt straight into the ninth heaven. The gods, Bajie, and Wujing did not understand what he meant. The monster flung them up and packed them all into the bag again; only Pilgrim escaped. The demon king withdrew his troops to the monastery and once again ordered ropes brought out so that the captives could be bound as before. Tang Sanzang, Bajie, and Wujing were hoisted high from the rafters; the white horse was tethered at the rear; and all the gods were likewise bound, carried into the cellar, and shut beneath its sealed cover. The fiends obeyed, putting everything away one by one; of this we shall say no more.

p.src: Now Sun Wukong, having leapt into the ninth heaven, had saved his life. When he saw the demon troops turn back without banners displayed, he knew that all the others had been captured. He lowered his auspicious cloud and landed on the summit of the eastern mountain, gnashing his teeth in hatred of the monster and shedding tears at the thought of Tang Sanzang. He raised his face to heaven, and in his grief suddenly wailed aloud. He cried, “Master! What hardships and misfortunes did you bring upon yourself in some former life, that in this life you meet a fiend at every step? If there is no escape from suffering such as this, what are we to do?” Alone, he sighed and lamented for a long while. Then he composed his spirit and pondered, asking himself, “What sort of bag can that demon possess, to hold so many things? Now it has swallowed up all those celestial gods and generals as well. I would seek help in Heaven, but I fear the Jade Emperor would blame me. I remember the True Warrior of the North, known as the Heavenly Honored One Who Quells Demons. He now dwells on Mount Wudang in the Southern Jambu Continent. I shall go and ask him to rescue Master from this calamity.” Indeed:
